city_tips.amsterdam: The hardest city to find a room. Start 4–6 months early and also look in Diemen, Amstelveen and Zaandam.
city_tips.rotterdam: Areas like Kralingen and Delfshaven are popular with students.
city_tips.utrecht: Sign up at ROOM.nl as soon as possible: your waiting time counts.
city_tips.den-haag: Also look in Rijswijk and Voorburg. They are close by tram.
city_tips.leiden: Few rooms and many students. Use DUWO short stay for your first months.
city_tips.delft: TU Delft has a housing office for international students. Contact them first.
city_tips.groningen: Cheaper than the Randstad, but many internationals arrive in September. Do not arrive without a room.
city_tips.eindhoven: Vestide is the main student housing provider. Register early.
city_tips.tilburg: Many rooms in private houses. Always check the landlord and the contract.
city_tips.den-bosch: Small city, so start looking early. Also check rooms in Vught and Rosmalen.
city_tips.nijmegen: SSH has many rooms near the Heyendaal campus.
city_tips.maastricht: Maastricht Housing is the official partner of the university.
city_tips.enschede: One of the cheapest student cities. You can also live on the UT campus.
city_tips.arnhem: Good train connection to Nijmegen if you study there.
city_tips.breda: BUas helps first-year international students with housing. Ask them first.

before.title: Before you arrive
items: Passport or ID card, valid for your whole stay
Birth certificate (with official stamp if needed)
Letter of acceptance from your school
Visa / residence permit arranged (non-EU only, via your school and the IND)
A room, or a place to stay for the first weeks
Enough money for the first months (rent, deposit, daily costs)
Travel or health insurance for the first weeks
Appointment at the city hall made online

first.title: Your first weeks
items: Register at the city hall
Get your BSN
Open a Dutch bank account
Apply for DigiD
Arrange health insurance (if you work)
Register with a general doctor (huisarts)
Get a public transport card (OV-chipkaart)
Buy a bike and a good lock

pay.title: Before you pay for a room
items: I have seen the room in real life or by live video call
I did a reverse image search on the photos
I checked the address on Google Maps
I know the full name of the landlord or agency
The agency is registered at the KvK (Chamber of Commerce)
I have a written contract
Registering at this address is allowed

before-0.why: You need a valid passport or ID card for your visa, the city hall, the bank and your rental contract.
steps: Check the expiry date: it must be valid for your whole stay.
Expires soon? Renew it in your home country before you leave. This can take weeks.
Make a photo or scan and keep it in a safe place (not in your email inbox).
before-0.tip: EU students can use an ID card. Non-EU students need a passport.

before-1.why: The city hall sometimes asks for your birth certificate when you register, to put your details in the Dutch population register (BRP).
steps: Ask for a recent copy of your birth certificate in your home country.
Check if it needs an official stamp (apostille or legalisation). This depends on your country.
From an EU country? Ask for a multilingual standard form. Then no stamp or translation is needed.
Not in English, Dutch, German or French? You may need a sworn translation.
before-1.tip: Arrange this early. It is very hard to do from the Netherlands.

before-2.why: Your letter of acceptance proves that you are a student. You need it for your visa, student housing and sometimes the bank.
steps: Download it from your school portal or email.
Save it as a PDF on your phone and print one copy.
Also save your proof of enrolment (inschrijving) once you have it.
before-2.tip: Housing providers like SSH or DUWO often ask for proof of enrolment.

before-3.why: Students from outside the EU/EEA/Switzerland usually need a residence permit to study in the Netherlands.
steps: From the EU/EEA or Switzerland? You do not need a visa. Skip this step.
Non-EU: your school applies for you at the IND. Ask the international office how it works.
Send your documents and pay the fee via your school.
After approval: pick up your MVV (entry visa) at the Dutch embassy, if you need one.
After arrival: pick up your residence permit card at the IND.
bring: Proof of enough money for your stay
before-3.cost: IND fee (check ind.nl for the current amount)
before-3.time: Start at least 3 months before you travel
before-3.tip: Do not book a non-refundable flight before your permit is approved.

before-4.why: Without an address you cannot register at the city hall, and without registration you get no BSN.
steps: Use the Rooms tab to compare cities and open housing websites.
Ask your school's housing office: they often have rooms for international students.
No room yet? Book a short stay (hostel, short-stay housing, HousingAnywhere) for your first weeks.
Do the scam check before you pay anything.
before-4.tip: Ask in the Community tab: other students may be looking for housemates.

before-5.why: In the first month you pay a lot at once: deposit, first rent, furniture, insurance and a bike.
steps: Use the Budget tool to see your monthly costs.
Count on a deposit of 1 month + the first rent + about €500 for start-up costs.
Bring a card that works abroad (Visa/Mastercard) until you have a Dutch account.
Check if you can get Dutch student finance (DUO) if you work in the Netherlands.
links: DUO – student finance for EU students
before-5.tip: Never pay rent in cash or with gift cards.

before-6.why: You must be insured from day one. Medical costs in the Netherlands can be very high.
steps: Check if your own insurance covers you in the Netherlands (EU students: bring your EHIC card).
Not covered? Take out a student insurance for international students for your first months.
Will you work in the Netherlands? Then you need Dutch health insurance (see To-do: health insurance).
before-6.tip: Keep your insurance card or policy on your phone.

before-7.why: Registering is required if you stay longer than 4 months. Appointments can be fully booked for weeks, so book early.
steps: Go to the website of the municipality (gemeente) where you will live.
Search for "registration" or "inschrijven" and book an appointment online.
Pick a date in your first week in the Netherlands.
Save the confirmation email.
before-7.tip: Some cities have a special desk for internationals with service in English.

first-0.why: Everyone who stays longer than 4 months must register at the municipality. This gives you a BSN.
steps: Go to your appointment at the city hall (gemeente).
Show your documents and fill in the form.
You often get your BSN at the desk, or by post within a few days.
bring: Rental contract or signed permission from your landlord
first-0.tip: Your landlord does not allow you to register? That is a red flag. Ask DutchDoor for help.

first-1.why: Your BSN (citizen service number) is your personal number for the government, the bank, work, the doctor and insurance.
steps: You get your BSN when you register at the city hall.
Write it down and keep the letter in a safe place.
Only give your BSN to official organisations (employer, bank, insurer, government).
first-1.time: Usually within a week after registering
first-1.tip: Never send a photo of your BSN or passport to a landlord you have not met.

first-2.why: Many shops, your rent and your salary need a Dutch or EU bank account. Many places do not accept credit cards.
steps: Choose a bank: ING, ABN AMRO, Rabobank (student accounts) or bunq (fully online).
Open the account online or make an appointment.
Show your passport and BSN. Some online banks let you start without a BSN.
Download the bank app and activate your debit card.
first-2.time: 1–2 weeks until you have your card
first-2.tip: Learn how iDEAL and Tikkie work: everyone uses them to pay and to split costs.

first-3.why: DigiD is your digital login for the government: taxes, healthcare allowance (zorgtoeslag), rent benefit and DUO.
steps: Go to digid.nl and click "Apply for DigiD".
Fill in your BSN, date of birth, postcode and house number.
You get an activation letter by post at your address within a few days.
Activate your DigiD and install the DigiD app.
first-3.tip: Your name must be on the mailbox, or the letter may not arrive.

first-4.why: Do you work in the Netherlands, even a small side job? Then Dutch basic health insurance (basisverzekering) is required by law.
steps: Check if you need it: working in the Netherlands = yes. Only studying = your own or a student insurance is often enough.
Compare insurers on a comparison website and choose a basic insurance.
Sign up within 4 months after you start working. You pay from the start date.
Low income? Apply for zorgtoeslag (healthcare allowance) with your DigiD.
first-4.cost: About €150 / month, partly paid back via zorgtoeslag
first-4.tip: You can get a fine if you work and have no Dutch insurance. Do not wait.

first-5.why: In the Netherlands you always go to your general doctor (huisarts) first. Register before you get sick.
steps: Search for "huisarts" + your postcode on Google Maps.
Call or check the website: do they accept new patients?
Fill in the registration form of the practice.
Many universities have a student doctor: ask your school.
first-5.time: It can take a few calls to find a place
first-5.tip: Emergency? Call 112. Urgent at night or at the weekend? Call the huisartsenpost (out-of-hours GP).

first-6.why: With an OV-chipkaart you travel by train, bus and tram. You can also check in with your bank card or phone.
steps: Easiest: check in and out with your contactless bank card or phone (OVpay).
Want discounts? Order a personal OV-chipkaart online.
Travel a lot? Add a discount subscription in the NS app.
Always check in AND check out, or you pay a high fee.
first-6.time: The card arrives in about 1 week
first-6.tip: EU students who work enough hours may get a free student travel product via DUO.

first-7.why: A bike is the cheapest and fastest way to get around in Dutch cities.
steps: Buy a second-hand bike: Marktplaats, Facebook groups or a local bike shop.
Or rent one: Swapfiets (monthly fee, repairs included).
Buy two good locks: a frame lock and a chain lock.
Learn the rules: lights on when it is dark, no phone while cycling.
first-7.tip: A very cheap bike from a stranger is often stolen. Do not buy it.

pay-0.why: Scammers often cannot show the room, because it does not exist or is not theirs.
steps: Ask for a viewing in real life, or a live video call (not a recorded video).
In the video call: ask them to show the street, the front door and the view from the window.
Ask the people who live there some questions.
pay-0.tip: "I am abroad and cannot show you the room" is the most common scam story.

pay-1.why: Scammers copy photos from other ads or from hotels.
steps: Save a photo from the ad.
Upload it to Google Lens or TinEye.
Do the same photos show up in another city or on another website? Then it is a scam.

pay-2.why: Fake ads sometimes use an address that does not exist, or the address of a shop or office.
steps: Search for the address on Google Maps.
Look at Street View: is it a house? Does it look like the photos?
Check the travel time to your school.

pay-3.why: You must know who you rent from. Scammers often only use a first name and WhatsApp.
steps: Ask for the full name of the landlord or the agency.
Search for the name online together with words like "scam" or "fraud".
Ask who owns the house. You can check this at the Kadaster (land registry) for a small fee.

pay-4.why: A real rental agency is registered at the Chamber of Commerce (KvK).
steps: Go to kvk.nl and search for the name of the agency.
Check that the address and KvK number match their website and contract.
Not registered? Do not pay.
pay-4.tip: An agency may not charge you agency fees if it also works for the landlord.

pay-5.why: A written contract protects you. Without one it is hard to prove anything.
steps: Ask for the contract before you pay anything.
Check: start date, length, rent, service costs, deposit and notice period.
Do you not understand something? Ask DutchDoor or your school to check it.
pay-5.tip: Pay the deposit by bank transfer, never in cash.

pay-6.why: Without registration at the city hall you get no BSN. Then you cannot work, open a bank account or get insurance.
steps: Ask the landlord in writing: "Can I register at this address?"
Make sure this is also in your contract.
Is the answer no? Look for another room.

scam: Is the rent much lower than normal for this city?
Is the landlord "abroad" or unable to show the room?
Do you have to pay before you have seen the room?
Do they ask for a copy of your passport very early?
Do they want payment by Western Union, crypto, gift cards or to a foreign bank?
Are they pushing you to decide today?
Do the photos look like a hotel, or do they show up elsewhere online?
Do they refuse a written contract, or say you cannot register at the address?
faq: How much does a room cost?
A room in a student house costs about €450–1,000 per month, depending on the city. A studio costs more. Use the Rooms tab to compare cities.
An interview with the people who already live in the house. They choose who gets the room. Be yourself and ask questions too.
How high can the deposit be?
There is a legal maximum (in most cases two months of basic rent). The landlord must pay it back after you move out. Check rijksoverheid.nl for the current rules.
Can I register at any address?
Only if the landlord allows it and the place is suitable to live in. Without registration you cannot get a BSN, so check this before you sign.
For many rooms the maximum rent depends on a points system. Do the free rent check of the Huurcommissie.
Do I need Dutch health insurance?
Usually yes if you have a job, even a small side job. If you only study, your own insurance or a student insurance may be enough.
steps: Know your budget
Use the budget tool to see what you can pay.
Start early
At least 3 months before you arrive.
Look in more places
Your school's housing office, Kamernet, Pararius, HousingAnywhere. Be careful in Facebook groups.
View the room
In real life or by live video call. Sometimes there is an interview with the housemates (hospiteren).
Check the contract
Length, rent, deposit, and is registration allowed?
Do the scam check
Before you pay anything.
Register your address
At the city hall, to get your BSN.
